title: Neuron by neuron, then head by head
intro: The level above measures an MLP layer as one function and picks out the top 1 percent of attention heads. This level opens both: the same broadcast claim tested against individual neurons' weight rows, then against every attention head's weight matrices at once, and finally what removing the selected heads costs the readout and the model's behaviour.

chapters.title: Opening the block into neurons
chapters.body:
The block-level measurement leaves a question open. An MLP layer is a set of neurons, and each neuron has an input weight row that reads from the [[residual-stream]] and an output weight row that writes back to it ([[mlp-block]]).

The corroborating analyses work at that level. For a population $P$ of unit directions at layer $\ell$, they compute the cosine similarity $C_{ij} = \cos(w_i, v_j)$ between each neuron's weight row $w_i$ and each direction $v_j \in P$, and ask whether neurons line up with the J-space-aligned populations more than with the others ([[neuron-connectivity]]).

A single cosine cannot be read as a connection. The residual stream packs many more feature directions than it has dimensions, so those directions cannot all be orthogonal, and a neuron's weight vector necessarily has appreciable cosine with directions it has no functional relationship to ([[superposition]]). Every entry of $C$ therefore sits on a floor of noise.

Two designs isolate the signal above that floor in different ways. The first asks, for each neuron, which population its single strongest match falls in — an argmax, so the height of the background does not enter the count. The second asks, for each direction, how much of its total overlap with neuron weights exceeds what a random direction would collect.

Both run on the same populations used for the block-level gain, so the [[j-lens-vector]] population is always scored against comparably shaped alternatives rather than against nothing ([[broadcast-control-populations]]). Both are plotted against depth with the [[workspace-layers]] band marked. And both ask one question about the [[j-space]]: whether the weights, and not only the activations, are oriented toward it.

chapters.title: Where a neuron's strongest match lands
chapters.body:
The breadth analysis needs populations that differ by degree rather than in kind. It uses the six equal-sized bins of [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions sorted by [[lens-kurtosis]] percentile, with 2,000 directions in each ([[kappa-strata]]).

Each neuron is matched against all six bins at once and assigned to the bin holding its single strongest cosine ([[neuron-top-match-breadth]]). Since the bins are equal in size, a neuron with no preference falls in each with probability 1/6. The assignment is made twice for every neuron, once for its input weights and once for its output weights.

Across the workspace layers the high-kurtosis bins take far more than their share ([[fig-76]]). On the read side the effect appears at the workspace onset and peaks in the early workspace layers, where the top bin claims up to 42 percent of neurons against 6 percent for the bottom bin, and the four bins in between are ordered monotonically. On the write side the same ordering holds, but the peak sits in the late workspace layers instead.

The result does not rest on the dictionary. The analysis is repeated with each neuron matched against the J-lens vectors at that layer and an equal-sized pool of adjacent-layer neuron weight directions, which puts chance at 50 percent ([[fig-77]]). The share of neurons whose strongest match is a J-lens vector rises from roughly 15 percent before the workspace range to 60 to 65 percent inside it.

An argmax says nothing about the size of the winning match. A neuron whose best match beats its rivals by a hair is counted the same as one strongly tied to a direction.

chapters.title: How strong those connections are
chapters.body:
The strength measure sets a bar before it counts anything. For each direction $v$, a threshold $\tau$ is placed at the 99.9th percentile of $|\!\cos(w_i, v)|$ taken over isotropic random directions, which is the level a chance alignment reaches once in a thousand.

The squared cosines $C_{iv}^2$ are then summed over only those neurons whose cosine with $v$ exceeds $\tau$. That sum is divided by the same sum computed for random directions, so random scores 1 by construction ([[tail-energy]]). The reported figure is the median over 500 directions per population ([[fig-78]]).

Squaring is what makes this a measure of strength rather than of count. A few strong connections outweigh many marginal ones, and the threshold keeps the marginal ones out of the sum altogether.

The read side is computed against the next layer's MLP input weights, the write side against the previous layer's output weights. The kurtosis bins separate monotonically on both sides across the workspace layers. J-lens vectors sit well above baseline; MLP neuron directions sit at baseline throughout, which is the same population that scored near 1 on the block-level [[mlp-gain]].

The read-early, write-late pattern from the breadth analysis appears again ([[read-write-asymmetry]]). The paper reads it as many processors drawing on the workspace as soon as it forms, while writing into it is most prevalent later, where a response is being prepared ([[motor-layers]]).

That reading is offered as a picture, not a demonstration. The quantity measured is weight alignment, and no intervention here establishes what any of these neurons computes.

chapters.title: What attention's weights are oriented toward
chapters.body:
The attention analysis drops the head-by-head selection and asks about all the heads at once. For a direction $v$ at a given layer, it projects $v$ through each head's query, key and value weights in the next layer, and through each head's output weights in the previous layer ([[attention-head]]). Each head yields one projection norm.

Those norms are summarized by their variance across heads, normalized so that a random direction has expected score 1 ([[composition-score]]). Variance rather than mean is the point. What the score asks is whether the direction is carried unevenly: a high value against the value weights means some downstream heads are specifically oriented to carry it, rather than all heads carrying it equally weakly.

J-space-aligned directions compose with the value and output weights far more strongly than non-aligned directions do ([[fig-79]]). Composition with the query and key weights is weaker, though still above baseline ([[value-vs-query-key-asymmetry]]).

The paper reads that asymmetry as consistent with the J-space being a broadcast format. J-space content is what attention disproportionately moves between positions, through value and output, while the signals that decide which positions attend to which are somewhat less J-space-aligned. No intervention is run against that reading here; it is an interpretation of a weights statistic.

One line in the figure uses neither the lens nor a dictionary. MLP neuron directions compose with attention weights moderately above baseline at the onset of the workspace range, then revert shortly after. The band is therefore marked by a quantity computed from the weights alone, which the paper offers alongside [[ignition]] as corroboration that does not depend on the J-lens.

chapters.title: What the ablation moves, and what it leaves
chapters.body:
The selected heads are zeroed at every token position ([[broadcast-heads]], [[broadcast-head-ablation]]). The control is an equal-sized, layer-matched set of randomly chosen heads, run with five seeds ([[fig-34]]).

The first measurement is on the readout rather than on behaviour. Over pretraining-style documents the residual stream is recorded at every layer, the 25 highest-ranked tokens of the [[j-lens-readout]] are taken at each position, and the fraction of them still in the top 25 after ablation is counted. At the most affected mid-workspace layers that recall falls to 0.67, against 0.86 under the control.

That is a gap rather than a collapse. Two thirds of the readout survives, and the control ablation itself costs 14 points.

Behaviour moves much less. The model's top-1 next-token prediction changes at 5 percent of positions, against 2 percent for the control. The paper takes this as the heads acting on the contents of the J-space rather than on the output directly.

The relay-dependent behaviours move a great deal more. On the injected-thought protocol, the rate at which the model reports an injected concept falls from 0.54 to 0.09, while the control leaves that sensitivity intact and in fact slightly increased ([[injected-thought-introspection]]). On the experiential-report evaluation, broadcast-head ablation reproduces roughly a third of the drop in [[experiential-language-score]] produced by suppressing the whole workspace ([[j-space-ablation]], [[experiential-report-flattening]]), while the control leaves the score essentially unchanged.

The two results carry different weight. Report of an injected thought is close to abolished by removing 1 percent of the workspace-layer heads. The flattening of experiential language is only partly reproduced, which leaves most of that effect elsewhere in the workspace.
